claim: Derek Yarmer's public record is built around local school-board oversight rather than a broad campaign-media operation. In his 2023 Hays Post questionnaire, he described himself as an ER doctor, a parent of children in USD 489, and a non-incumbent candidate whose campaign was "100 percent personally financed." claim: The clearest throughline in Yarmer's board messaging is fiscal scrutiny. In his 2023 questionnaire, he said the board has "the absolute responsibility" to keep the $143.5 million bond project on budget and deliver the school structures promised to the community. In a 2025 written statement published by Hays Post, he argued that the district was using capital outlay funds for items that should be covered by the bond, criticized spending on a concession stand, scoreboards, tennis courts, and a marquee sign while other building needs waited, and wrote that the school board was also to blame for "reckless spending" because it failed to provide proper oversight. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/52e53c90-5182-42f0-919e-2c7dc145305b)

claim: His process critique is just as consistent as the spending critique. As a candidate, he said all school board meetings should be broadcast, agendas should be released at least a week in advance, and board members should be able to add items easily. As a board member, he repeatedly objected to receiving large purchase numbers and voting the same night. Tiger Media Network quoted him in 2025 saying, "This would be an example of giving us the numbers and voting on it the same night, which I'm against," and in 2026 saying purchases over $100,000 should be discussed at the prior board meeting before a vote. claim: Yarmer's oversight posture also shows up in personnel and contract discussions. At his first 2024 board meeting, he abstained from extending administrator contracts after a short executive session, saying, "You're asking me to vote on something I know nothing about." claim: On education policy, Yarmer's public comments emphasize core academics, leaner operations, and skepticism of expansive school roles. claim:
narrative: "*A summary of what Derek Yarmer has publicly said, written, and been quoted saying in campaign questionnaires, a published written statement, USD 489 board coverage, school/public pages, and professional profiles through 2026-05-11. No verified campaign website or public candidate-controlled social account was found. We report patterns; we do not interpret intent.*

---

Derek Yarmer's public record is built around local school-board oversight rather than a broad campaign-media operation. In his 2023 Hays Post questionnaire, he described himself as an ER doctor, a parent of children in USD 489, and a non-incumbent candidate whose campaign was "100 percent personally financed." He said he thought there were "a lot of great things going on within the district," including new facilities, but framed his main goal as making sure Hays residents got "the new schools they were promised at the price they were promised." [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/0ef676f6-e0ff-4a1c-b697-d9f74d3d7649)

His earliest accessible school-board statement, a 2021 application letter for a vacant USD 489 seat, presented education as a parental responsibility and community duty. He wrote that educating children is "one of the most important responsibilities we have as parents," said he wanted to be active in his daughters' education and the education of other district students, and argued that his emergency-medicine background could help the district take a pragmatic approach to pandemic decisions while keeping interruptions to education low. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/f743144f-86f5-409f-af1d-729253115b28)

The clearest throughline in Yarmer's board messaging is fiscal scrutiny. In his 2023 questionnaire, he said the board has "the absolute responsibility" to keep the $143.5 million bond project on budget and deliver the school structures promised to the community. In a 2025 written statement published by Hays Post, he argued that the district was using capital outlay funds for items that should be covered by the bond, criticized spending on a concession stand, scoreboards, tennis courts, and a marquee sign while other building needs waited, and wrote that the school board was also to blame for "reckless spending" because it failed to provide proper oversight. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/52e53c90-5182-42f0-919e-2c7dc145305b)

His process critique is just as consistent as the spending critique. As a candidate, he said all school board meetings should be broadcast, agendas should be released at least a week in advance, and board members should be able to add items easily. As a board member, he repeatedly objected to receiving large purchase numbers and voting the same night. Tiger Media Network quoted him in 2025 saying, "This would be an example of giving us the numbers and voting on it the same night, which I'm against," and in 2026 saying purchases over $100,000 should be discussed at the prior board meeting before a vote. [Source](https://tigermedianet.com/?p=90779) [Source](https://tigermedianet.com/?p=94701)

Yarmer's oversight posture also shows up in personnel and contract discussions. At his first 2024 board meeting, he abstained from extending administrator contracts after a short executive session, saying, "You're asking me to vote on something I know nothing about." In 2026 coverage, he supported delaying district contract-extension votes for more review, flagged superintendent contract language that appeared to make the superintendent his own supervisor, and moved to vote on administrator contracts individually. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/95dab7ab-70ba-44ee-91ee-2760e55665bf) [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/0c27e966-61e9-4c00-b6d7-7f37f6d3bba7) [Source](https://tigermedianet.com/?p=95549)

On education policy, Yarmer's public comments emphasize core academics, leaner operations, and skepticism of expansive school roles. During a 2025 discussion of special education funding and district spending, he said the district could "work a little leaner," questioned whether requested items were needs, and said, "I don't think money is the problem of the education system. I think we need to be better at doing what we do." In the same meeting coverage, he criticized social-emotional and mental-health programming and said schools should teach "math, science and history" rather than be "touchy-feely." [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/753ae9c5-9a0b-4bc2-b319-57e7fc4efdeb)

His public safety and facility comments are usually tied back to practical oversight. In 2026, he asked whether Felten Elementary plumbing had been scoped before bidding, saying it is good to know what a project involves before going into it. In Hays High bathroom and vandalism coverage, he said cameras outside bathrooms were not adequate for safety or security purposes. In asbestos-abatement coverage, he seconded a motion to table and said, "If everything is an emergency, nothing is an emergency." [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/f5e69fbd-0165-4db1-b896-07613f7a31ed) [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/7b63aeb8-e2d2-40a4-af96-5e92884d3ede) [Source](https://tigermedianet.com/?p=93176)

His medical background is part of the public persona, but the political messaging remains local and operational. HaysMed identifies him as an Emergency Department physician trained at the University of Kansas School of Medicine and the University of Missouri-Kansas City. Pawnee Valley Community Hospital's 2023 announcement of him as Emergency Department medical director quotes him saying PVCH was "well-equipped to care for patients" and that he hoped to help provide quality care to central and western Kansas by offering guidance and support when needed. [Source](https://www.haysmed.com/provider/derek-m-yarmer-md/) [Source](https://pawneevalleyhospital.com/dr-yarmer-new-ed-medical-director-at-pawnee-valley-community-hospital/)

The visible absences matter. I did not verify a current campaign website, public candidate-controlled social account, campaign video channel, endorsement page, donation page, or long-form civic platform. The accessible record also did not show substantial candidate-authored messaging on state or national partisan issues, school vouchers, library policy, curriculum culture-war topics beyond the quoted social-emotional-learning discussion, teacher unions, school finance formulas beyond special education and local mill levies, or non-school local government issues. This is a limitation of the accessible public record, not a claim about private, deleted, restricted, or unindexed content.

Methodology: Sources checked included USD 489 official pages and meeting portal, Hays Post, Tiger Media Network, BoardDocs search results, HaysMed, Pawnee Valley Community Hospital, Great Bend Tribune, and web searches for campaign, civic, professional, and social accounts. Date range covered: public material available through 2026-05-11. Public social harvest: no verified candidate-controlled social posts were found, so no inaccessible social content was fabricated or summarized. We report patterns in public, candidate-controlled or attributed messaging; we do not interpret intent.",

claim:
narrative: "*A summary of what Allen Park has publicly said, written, and been quoted saying in campaign questionnaires, USD 489 official pages, local board coverage, and civic media through 2026-05-11. No verified campaign website or public candidate-controlled social account was found. We report patterns; we do not interpret intent.*

---

Allen Park's public messaging is rooted in his long history inside USD 489. In 2023, he described himself as a retired elementary principal, licensed insurance agent, part-time UPS worker, and incumbent board member. He said he came from a family of educators, that his wife Patti had also spent decades in education, and that his own USD 489 work included paraprofessional, teacher, coach, migrant director, transition coordinator, and 25 years as Washington Elementary principal. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/ba82fc30-cb69-4a6d-8f09-c3ec5d9d51a7)

The core phrase in Park's campaign record is "kids and families first." He used that framing in 2019 when he told KLC Journal he wanted to be part of a school-board team with that priority, and he returned to it in 2023 when he said he would use it as a reference point for decisions. His related test for school decisions was whether they are best for kids. [Source](https://klcjournal.com/local2019hays/) [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/ba82fc30-cb69-4a6d-8f09-c3ec5d9d51a7)

Park's most consistent theme is trust through communication. In 2019, he said USD 489 needed to reconnect with the Hays community by rebuilding trust, encouraging involvement, increasing communication, and genuinely listening. In his 2023 Q&A, he again identified communication as the main thing he would change, saying minority opinions should be heard and board meetings should be inclusive and transparent. [Source](https://klcjournal.com/local2019hays/) [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/7acb9e0e-4c56-4e6f-a618-4312a49cd922)

Facilities and bond oversight are another major throughline. Before joining the board, Park said he had supported prior bond issues and wanted community, teacher, and staff input in planning. After the $143.5 million bond passed, he framed the work as unfinished: residents needed information, answers, and chances to give input on how their investment was being spent. He said the board had to ensure the bond process was done correctly, on time, and fiscally responsibly. [Source](https://archive.hayspost.com/2019/06/page/37/) [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/7acb9e0e-4c56-4e6f-a618-4312a49cd922)

His facilities comments often combine support for school investment with questions about process and cost. In USD 489's 2022 bond article, Park asked how much a special election would cost, raised concerns about replacing a two-section elementary school with a four-section school, asked about school choice under realignment, and asked about using local contractors. In 2025 property-sale coverage, he asked why the district was moving quickly, wanted an appraisal, and questioned the value of water rights. [Source](https://www.usd489.com/article/651221) [Source](https://tigermedianet.com/?p=92038)

Park also presents fiscal responsibility as a board duty tied to student outcomes. In 2023, he said he would keep asking budget questions and connect spending decisions to academic achievement. He also said he would look for local purchasing, appropriate cuts, grant writing, community partnerships, and efficient use of district facilities. In 2019, his published goals included fiscal soundness, safe facilities, local businesses, and data-informed decisions. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/ba82fc30-cb69-4a6d-8f09-c3ec5d9d51a7) [Source](https://archive.hayspost.com/2019/06/page/37/)

On board role and administration, Park's stated position is policy governance rather than day-to-day management. In the 2023 Q&A, he said the board writes policy, should make sure policy follows state law, and should clearly communicate expectations, but daily management is not the board's job. He also said administrators need tools, guidance, and expectations from the board. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/7acb9e0e-4c56-4e6f-a618-4312a49cd922)

His board record shows repeated interest in process, minutes, personnel review, and policy clarity. In 2023, he argued board minutes should include more detail about why members vote no, though the board attorney said Kansas law did not require that. In the same year, he objected with Curt Vajnar to hiring the superintendent's wife and later asked the board to review whether the district was following its nepotism policy. [Source](https://greatbendpost.com/posts/11e68e53-1cdc-4676-afb0-aef5b6ee450e) [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/9fb91da0-f9e5-4d80-a065-c5c2727c6fb8)

Park's education-policy messaging is local and operational, not partisan. He has publicly supported technology needs and teacher training, smaller or manageable class sizes, reduced student fees, strong staff, safe facilities, and professional learning for board members. During a 2024 calendar discussion, he asked whether the district was giving parents support on student days off, then voted against the calendar with Derek Yarmer. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/ba82fc30-cb69-4a6d-8f09-c3ec5d9d51a7) [Source](https://www.usd489.com/article/1447496)

His campaign-finance answer was limited and local. In 2023, he said he had not received money from outside the school district, that the few donations he received came from family, friends, and community members who care about kids and education in Hays, and that additional expenses were paid personally. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/7acb9e0e-4c56-4e6f-a618-4312a49cd922)

The visible absences matter. I did not verify a current campaign website, public candidate-controlled social account, campaign video channel, endorsement page, donation page, or long-form platform. The accessible record also did not show substantial candidate-authored messaging on state or national partisan issues, religion, abortion, guns, immigration, vouchers, library policy, or federal politics. This is a limitation of the accessible public record, not a claim about private, deleted, restricted, or unindexed content.

Methodology: Sources checked included USD 489 official pages and meeting portal, Hays Post, Hays Post archive, Great Bend Post, Tiger Media Network, KLC Journal, BoardDocs-style search results, and web searches for campaign, civic, professional, and social accounts. Date range covered: public material available through 2026-05-11. Public social harvest: no verified candidate-controlled social posts were found, so no inaccessible social content was fabricated or summarized. We report patterns in public, candidate-controlled or attributed messaging; we do not interpret intent.",
exactEvidenceSummary:
narrative: "*A summary of what Allen Park has publicly said, written, and been quoted saying in campaign questionnaires, USD 489 official pages, local board coverage, and civic media through 2026-05-11. No verified campaign website or public candidate-controlled social account was found. We report patterns; we do not interpret intent.*

---

Allen Park's public messaging is rooted in his long history inside USD 489. In 2023, he described himself as a retired elementary principal, licensed insurance agent, part-time UPS worker, and incumbent board member. He said he came from a family of educators, that his wife Patti had also spent decades in education, and that his own USD 489 work included paraprofessional, teacher, coach, migrant director, transition coordinator, and 25 years as Washington Elementary principal. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/ba82fc30-cb69-4a6d-8f09-c3ec5d9d51a7)

The core phrase in Park's campaign record is "kids and families first." He used that framing in 2019 when he told KLC Journal he wanted to be part of a school-board team with that priority, and he returned to it in 2023 when he said he would use it as a reference point for decisions. His related test for school decisions was whether they are best for kids. [Source](https://klcjournal.com/local2019hays/) [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/ba82fc30-cb69-4a6d-8f09-c3ec5d9d51a7)

Park's most consistent theme is trust through communication. In 2019, he said USD 489 needed to reconnect with the Hays community by rebuilding trust, encouraging involvement, increasing communication, and genuinely listening. In his 2023 Q&A, he again identified communication as the main thing he would change, saying minority opinions should be heard and board meetings should be inclusive and transparent. [Source](https://klcjournal.com/local2019hays/) [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/7acb9e0e-4c56-4e6f-a618-4312a49cd922)

Facilities and bond oversight are another major throughline. Before joining the board, Park said he had supported prior bond issues and wanted community, teacher, and staff input in planning. After the $143.5 million bond passed, he framed the work as unfinished: residents needed information, answers, and chances to give input on how their investment was being spent. He said the board had to ensure the bond process was done correctly, on time, and fiscally responsibly. [Source](https://archive.hayspost.com/2019/06/page/37/) [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/7acb9e0e-4c56-4e6f-a618-4312a49cd922)

His facilities comments often combine support for school investment with questions about process and cost. In USD 489's 2022 bond article, Park asked how much a special election would cost, raised concerns about replacing a two-section elementary school with a four-section school, asked about school choice under realignment, and asked about using local contractors. In 2025 property-sale coverage, he asked why the district was moving quickly, wanted an appraisal, and questioned the value of water rights. [Source](https://www.usd489.com/article/651221) [Source](https://tigermedianet.com/?p=92038)

Park also presents fiscal responsibility as a board duty tied to student outcomes. In 2023, he said he would keep asking budget questions and connect spending decisions to academic achievement. He also said he would look for local purchasing, appropriate cuts, grant writing, community partnerships, and efficient use of district facilities. In 2019, his published goals included fiscal soundness, safe facilities, local businesses, and data-informed decisions. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/ba82fc30-cb69-4a6d-8f09-c3ec5d9d51a7) [Source](https://archive.hayspost.com/2019/06/page/37/)

On board role and administration, Park's stated position is policy governance rather than day-to-day management. In the 2023 Q&A, he said the board writes policy, should make sure policy follows state law, and should clearly communicate expectations, but daily management is not the board's job. He also said administrators need tools, guidance, and expectations from the board. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/7acb9e0e-4c56-4e6f-a618-4312a49cd922)

His board record shows repeated interest in process, minutes, personnel review, and policy clarity. In 2023, he argued board minutes should include more detail about why members vote no, though the board attorney said Kansas law did not require that. In the same year, he objected with Curt Vajnar to hiring the superintendent's wife and later asked the board to review whether the district was following its nepotism policy. [Source](https://greatbendpost.com/posts/11e68e53-1cdc-4676-afb0-aef5b6ee450e) [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/9fb91da0-f9e5-4d80-a065-c5c2727c6fb8)

Park's education-policy messaging is local and operational, not partisan. He has publicly supported technology needs and teacher training, smaller or manageable class sizes, reduced student fees, strong staff, safe facilities, and professional learning for board members. During a 2024 calendar discussion, he asked whether the district was giving parents support on student days off, then voted against the calendar with Derek Yarmer. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/ba82fc30-cb69-4a6d-8f09-c3ec5d9d51a7) [Source](https://www.usd489.com/article/1447496)

His campaign-finance answer was limited and local. In 2023, he said he had not received money from outside the school district, that the few donations he received came from family, friends, and community members who care about kids and education in Hays, and that additional expenses were paid personally. [Source](https://hayspost.com/posts/7acb9e0e-4c56-4e6f-a618-4312a49cd922)

The visible absences matter. I did not verify a current campaign website, public candidate-controlled social account, campaign video channel, endorsement page, donation page, or long-form platform. The accessible record also did not show substantial candidate-authored messaging on state or national partisan issues, religion, abortion, guns, immigration, vouchers, library policy, or federal politics. This is a limitation of the accessible public record, not a claim about private, deleted, restricted, or unindexed content.

**Methodology:** Sources checked included USD 489 official pages and meeting portal, Hays Post, Hays Post archive, Great Bend Post, Tiger Media Network, KLC Journal, BoardDocs-style search results, and web searches for campaign, civic, professional, and social accounts. Date range covered: public material available through 2026-05-11. Public social harvest: no verified candidate-controlled social posts were found, so no inaccessible social content was fabricated or summarized.
